{{Short description|Set of values for a mathematical model}}
The '''parameter space''' is the [[Space (mathematics)|space]] of all possible parameter values that define a particular [[mathematical model]]. It is also sometimes called '''weight space''', and is often a [[subset]] of finite-dimensional [[Euclidean space]].

In [[statistics]], parameter spaces are particularly useful for describing [[Parametric family|parametric families]] of [[probability distribution]]s. They also form the background for [[parameter estimation]]. In the case of [[extremum estimator]]s for [[parametric model]]s, a certain [[objective function]] is maximized or minimized over the parameter space.<ref name="Hayashi p446">{{cite book |first=Fumio |last=Hayashi |author-link=Fumio Hayashi |title=Econometrics |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2000 |page=446 |isbn=0-691-01018-8 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QyIW8WUIyzcC&pg=PA446 }}</ref> Theorems of [[Existence theorem|existence]] and [[Consistent estimator|consistency]] of such estimators require some assumptions about the [[topology]] of the parameter space. For instance, [[compactness]] of the parameter space, together with [[Continuous function|continuity]] of the objective function, suffices for the existence of an extremum estimator.<ref name="Hayashi p446" />

Sometimes, parameters are analyzed to view how they affect their statistical model. In that context, they can be viewed as inputs of a [[function (mathematics)|function]], in which case the technical term for the parameter space is [[domain of a function]]. The ranges of values of the parameters may form the axes of a [[Plot (graphics)|plot]], and particular outcomes of the model may be plotted against these axes to illustrate how different regions of the parameter space produce different types of behavior in the model.

==Examples==
* A simple model of health deterioration after developing [[lung cancer]] could include the two parameters gender<ref name=one>{{Cite journal |last=Gasperino |first=J. |author2=Rom, W. N. |year=2004 |title=Gender and lung cancer |journal=Clinical Lung Cancer |volume=5 |issue=6 |pages=353–359 |doi= 10.3816/CLC.2004.n.013|pmid= 15217534}}</ref> and smoker/non-smoker, in which case the parameter space is the following set of four possibilities: {{math|{(Male, Smoker), (Male, Non-smoker), (Female, Smoker), (Female, Non-smoker)} }}.
* The [[logistic map]] <math> x_{n+1} = r x_n (1-x_n) </math> has one parameter, ''r'', which can take any positive value. The parameter space is therefore [[positive real numbers]]. 
:For some values of ''r'', this function ends up cycling around a few values or becomes fixed on one value. These long-term values can be plotted against ''r'' in a [[bifurcation diagram]] to show the different behaviours of the function for different values of ''r''.

* In a [[sine wave]] model <math>y(t) = A \cdot \sin(\omega t + \phi),</math> the parameters are [[amplitude]] ''A'' > 0, [[angular frequency]] ω > 0, and [[phase (waves)|phase]] φ ∈ S<sup>1</sup>. Thus the parameter space is <math>R^+ \times R^+ \times S^1 .</math>
* In [[complex dynamics]], the parameter space is the [[complex plane]] '''C''' = { ''z'' = ''x'' + ''y'' i : x, y ∈ '''R''' }, where i<sup>2</sup> = &minus;1.

:The famous [[Mandelbrot set]] is a [[subset]] of this parameter space, consisting of the points <math>c</math> in the complex plane which give a [[bounded set]] of numbers when a [[iterated function]] <math>z_{n+1} = f_c(z_n) = z^2+c</math> is repeatedly applied from that starting point <math>z_0 = 0</math>. The remaining points, which are not in the set, give an unbounded set of numbers (they tend to infinity) when this function is repeatedly applied from that <math>z_0</math>.

* In [[machine learning]], [[hyperparameter (machine learning)|hyperparameters]] are used to describe models. In [[deep learning]], the parameters of a deep network are called '''weights.''' Due to the layered structure of deep networks, their weight space has a complex structure and geometry.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Navon |first1=Aviv |last2=Shamsian |first2=Aviv |last3=Achituve |first3=Idan |last4=Fetaya |first4=Ethan |last5=Chechik |first5=Gal |last6=Maron |first6=Haggai |date=2023-07-03 |title=Equivariant Architectures for Learning in Deep Weight Spaces |url=https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/navon23a.html |journal=Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning |language=en |publisher=PMLR |pages=25790–25816|arxiv=2301.12780 }}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Hecht-Nielsen |first=Robert |chapter=ON THE ALGEBRAIC STRUCTURE OF FEEDFORWARD NETWORK WEIGHT SPACES |date=1990-01-01 |chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780444884008500194 |title=Advanced Neural Computers |pages=129–135 |editor-last=Eckmiller |editor-first=Rolf |access-date=2023-12-01 |place=Amsterdam |publisher=North-Holland |isbn=978-0-444-88400-8}}</ref> For example, in [[multilayer perceptrons]], the same function is preserved when [[Permutation|permuting]] the nodes of a hidden layer, amounting to permuting weight matrices of the network. This property is known as ''[[equivariance]] to permutation'' of deep weight spaces.<ref name=":0" /> The study seeks [[hyperparameter optimization]].

==History==
Parameter space contributed to the liberation of [[geometry]] from the confines of [[three-dimensional space]]. For instance, the parameter space of [[sphere (geometry)|spheres]] in three dimensions, has four dimensions—three for the sphere center and another for the radius.  According to [[Dirk Struik]], it was the book ''Neue Geometrie des Raumes'' (1849) by [[Julius Plücker]] that showed
<blockquote>...geometry need not solely be based on points as basic elements. Lines, planes, circles, spheres can all be used as the elements (''Raumelemente'') on which a geometry can be based. This fertile conception threw new light on both synthetic and algebraic geometry and created new forms of duality. The number of dimensions of a particular form of geometry could now be any positive number, depending on the number of parameters necessary to define the "element".<ref name=DS>[[Dirk Struik]] (1967) ''A Concise History of Mathematics'', 3rd edition, [[Dover Books]]</ref>{{rp|165}}</blockquote>
The requirement for higher dimensions is illustrated by [[Plücker coordinates|Plücker's line geometry]]. Struik writes
<blockquote>[Plücker's] geometry of lines in three-space could be considered as a four-dimensional geometry, or, as [[Felix Klein|Klein]] has stressed, as the geometry of a four-dimensional [[quadric]] in a five-dimensional space.<ref name=DS/>{{rp|168}}</blockquote>
Thus the [[Klein quadric]] describes the parameters of lines in space.
